bookTitle: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets

facts.statement: A percentage retracement is a corrective countertrend price movement against the prevailing major, secondary, or near-term trend that retraces a predictable portion of the prior impulse move before resuming the original trend direction.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: Following a market move, prices consistently retrace a portion of the previous trend before resuming their move in the original direction.

facts.statement: Combining Dow Theory thirds with Fibonacci ratios establishes two primary correction bands: a minimum retracement zone between 33% and 38.2%, an intermediate 50% halfway mark, and a critical maximum retracement zone between 61.8% and 66%.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: Combining Dow and Fibonacci methodologies establishes two primary bands: a Minimum Retracement Zone (33%–38%) and a Maximum Retracement Zone (62%–66%).

facts.statement: Retracement price targets are calculated by multiplying the total vertical price range of the prior trend by standard Dow or Fibonacci retracement ratios and subtracting from the peak in an uptrend or adding to the trough in a downtrend.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: P_retrace = P_high - [ R * (P_high - P_low) ] and P_retrace = P_low + [ R * (P_high - P_low) ]

formulaDetails.name: Uptrend and Downtrend Retracement Formula
formulaDetails.latex: P_{\text{retrace, up}} = P_{\text{high}} - \left[ R \times (P_{\text{high}} - P_{\text{low}}) \right], \quad P_{\text{retrace, down}} = P_{\text{low}} + \left[ R \times (P_{\text{high}} - P_{\text{low}}) \right]

variables.definition: Peak price of the prior impulse trend
Trough price of the prior impulse trend

facts.statement: Fibonacci retracement percentages derive from the mathematical relationships within the Fibonacci sequence: consecutive numbers yield the 61.8% maximum ratio (such as 8/13 = 0.615 or 13/21 = 0.619), while alternate numbers yield the 38.2% minimum ratio (such as 13/34 = 0.382 or 1 - 0.618).

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: 38.2% = Ratio of alternate Fibonacci numbers (e.g., 13/34 ≈ 0.382 or 1 - 0.618); 61.8% = Ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers (e.g., 8/13 ≈ 0.615, 13/21 ≈ 0.619).

facts.statement: A healthy trend correction must hold above the 62% to 66% maximum retracement zone; if price decisively violates the 66% two-thirds threshold, the move fails as a correction and signals a full trend reversal expected to retrace 100% back to the prior trend origin.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: If price moves decisively beyond the two-thirds (66%) or 62% retracement point, the move is no longer considered a correction; the odds favor a full trend reversal that typically retraces 100% of the prior trend.

facts.statement: Traders establish initial trend-following entries in the 33%–50% or 38%–50% retracement zones, utilize the 62%–66% boundary as a tight low-risk execution area, and place protective stop-loss orders just beyond the 66% line or the 100% trend origin.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: The 62%–66% level represents a low-risk buying area in an uptrend... Place protective stops just beyond the 66% retracement line or just past the origin of the prior move (100% level).

facts.statement: During the April to August 1997 uptrend in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, three consecutive daily corrections respected Fibonacci bands: the first pullback held at 38%, the second bottomed at 62%, and the third stabilized near 50%.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: Dow measured from its April low to August high respected Fibonacci levels: the first decline held at the 38% line, the second hit the 62% line, and the third stopped near 50%.

facts.statement: On monthly and weekly U.S. Treasury Bond futures charts, the 1994 price collapse halted precisely at the 38% Fibonacci retracement of the 1981–1993 secular bull market, while the subsequent 1996 decline held exactly at the 62% retracement of the 1994–1996 advance.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: The 1994 price collapse in T-Bonds halted exactly at the 38% Fibonacci retracement of the entire 1981–1993 bull market. In a subsequent cycle, the 1996 decline corrected precisely to the 62% retracement line.

facts.statement: Developed by Edson Gould, speed resistance lines (speedlines) combine trendlines with one-third and two-thirds vertical percentage retracements, projecting two fan-shaped angular lines directly through price action to measure the rate of trend ascent or descent.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: Developed by Edson Gould, speed resistance lines combine trendlines with percentage retracements by dividing the vertical height of a move into thirds... measure the rate of ascent or descent (speed).

facts.statement: Speedlines divide the vertical height between trend origin and extreme into one-third and two-thirds vertical levels, projecting angular lines from the origin coordinate through those two vertical division points aligned at the peak or trough date.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: Calculate vertical range: V = P_high - P_start. Calculate two-thirds point: P_2/3 = P_start + (2/3)V. Calculate one-third point: P_1/3 = P_start + (1/3)V.

formulaDetails.name: Bullish and Bearish Speedline Coordinates
formulaDetails.latex: V = |P_{\text{extreme}} - P_{\text{start}}|, \quad P_{2/3, \text{bull}} = P_{\text{start}} + \frac{2}{3}V, \quad P_{1/3, \text{bull}} = P_{\text{start}} + \frac{1}{3}V, \quad P_{2/3, \text{bear}} = P_{\text{start}} - \frac{2}{3}V, \quad P_{1/3, \text{bear}} = P_{\text{start}} - \frac{1}{3}V

variables.definition: Total vertical price range from trend origin to current extreme
Starting price at the origin of the trend at time T_1
Highest peak in an uptrend or lowest trough in a downtrend at time T_2
Vertical coordinate for the upper 2/3 speedline at time T_2
Vertical coordinate for the lower 1/3 speedline at time T_2

facts.statement: Because speedlines measure the evolving geometry of an active trend, whenever an uptrend establishes a new higher peak or a downtrend establishes a new lower trough, all vertical thirds must be recalculated and both speedlines redrawn from the origin.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: Every time price sets a new high in an uptrend (or a new low in a downtrend), all speedlines must be redrawn using the new peak or trough.

facts.statement: During an uptrend pullback, price should initially hold support at the upper 2/3 speedline; if the 2/3 line breaks, price falls to test the lower 1/3 speedline, and a violation of the 1/3 line signals a complete retracement back to the trend origin.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: Downward corrections in an uptrend should hold at the upper (2/3) speedline. If the 2/3 line breaks, price typically falls to test the lower (1/3) speedline. If the lower (1/3) line breaks, prices will likely decline all the way to the beginning of the prior trend.

facts.statement: Once a speedline is decisively penetrated on a pullback, its technical polarity reverses: in an uptrend, a broken 2/3 support speedline turns into an overhead resistance barrier during subsequent rallies off the lower 1/3 speedline.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: Once broken, a speedline reverses its role (e.g., a broken 2/3 support line becomes an overhead resistance line on subsequent bounces).

facts.statement: Traders buy reaction pullbacks near the upper 2/3 speedline in an uptrend, liquidate long positions immediately if the 2/3 line breaks to target the 1/3 line, and treat the broken 2/3 line as resistance on bounces from the 1/3 line.

sourceCitation.book: Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets
sourceCitation.chapter: Retracements, Speedlines, Reversal Days & Price Gaps
sourceCitation.excerpt: Buy reaction pullbacks near the higher 2/3 speedline in an uptrend. If the 2/3 line breaks, exit long positions and target the 1/3 speedline.

generalAssumptions: Market action discounts all known and unknown fundamentals.
Prices move in trends, and a trend in motion is more likely to continue than to reverse.
Countertrend corrections Across major, secondary, and near-term degrees unfold in proportional geometric ratios of the preceding impulse wave.
